summary:
Workplace Insight reports on polling commissioned by Careerminds UK covering 600 UK full-time employees, examining attitudes toward replacing human line managers with AI.

Headline finding: 36.7 percent of employees said an AI manager would make them more productive, while 25.5 percent expected a decline and 37.8 percent said it would make no difference. However, when asked who they would prefer performance feedback from, 74.2 percent chose their human line manager versus 14.2 percent choosing AI, with 11.7 percent expressing no preference. The report frames this as openness to AI absorbing management functions but not the human relational aspects.

Seniority is the strongest dividing line. 64 percent of director-level and above respondents said an AI manager would boost productivity, including 28 percent expecting a significant increase, compared with 42.6 percent of senior employees, 38.5 percent of managers, 27.6 percent of mid-level and 26.2 percent of entry-level staff. Just over half of entry-level workers expected no difference. On feedback, 26 percent of directors and above would prefer AI versus 8 percent of mid-level workers.

Age also divides opinion: 50.6 percent of 25 to 34 year olds expected productivity gains versus 14.4 percent of 55 to 64 year olds. Preference for AI feedback fell from 18.2 percent among 25 to 34s to 8.9 percent among 55 to 64s, with no respondents aged 61 or above choosing AI. Gender differences were smaller.

Context cited includes CMI research that 82 percent of UK managers receive no formal management or leadership training, and a Gartner prediction that through 2026 one in five organisations will use AI to flatten structures, potentially eliminating more than half of middle-management roles.

Amanda Augustine of Careerminds UK cautioned against reading the data as a desire to replace managers, noting middle managers are squeezed between senior leadership expectations and team needs, and that employees still value human judgement and context.

claims.claim: More than a third of UK employees believe replacing their line manager with AI would improve their productivity
claims.attribution: Careerminds UK polling of 600 UK full-time employees

claims.claim: A quarter of employees expected productivity to decline under an AI manager
Employees expecting no productivity difference from an AI manager
A large majority prefer performance feedback from their human line manager
claims.stat: 74.2 percent versus 14.2 percent preferring AI, 11.7 percent no preference

claims.claim: Enthusiasm for AI management rises with seniority
claims.stat: 64 percent of directors and above, including 28 percent expecting a significant increase; 42.6 percent senior employees; 38.5 percent managers; 27.6 percent mid-level; 26.2 percent entry-level

claims.claim: Senior staff are more willing to receive AI feedback
claims.stat: 26 percent of directors and above versus 8 percent of mid-level workers

claims.claim: Younger employees are more positive about AI management
claims.stat: 50.6 percent of 25-34 year olds versus 14.4 percent of 55-64 year olds

claims.claim: Preference for AI-delivered feedback declines with age
claims.stat: 18.2 percent of 25-34s versus 8.9 percent of 55-64s; zero among respondents aged 61 or above

claims.claim: Gender differences in expectations were small
claims.stat: 37.3 percent of men versus 35.8 percent of women expected productivity gains; 28 percent of women versus 23.6 percent of men expected a decline; 16.6 percent of men versus 10.9 percent of women preferred AI feedback

claims.claim: Most UK managers receive no formal management or leadership training before taking up their roles
Through 2026, one in five organisations will use AI to flatten organisational structures, potentially eliminating more than half of existing middle-management positions
claims.stat: one in five organisations; more than 50 percent of middle-management roles

claims.claim: Employees seeing productivity gains from AI should not be read as wanting managers replaced; middle managers are squeezed between senior leader expectations and team needs
claims.attribution: Amanda Augustine, resident careers expert, Careerminds UK

claims.claim: Seniority differences may reflect leaders viewing AI through an efficiency and decision-making lens while earlier-career staff focus on day-to-day guidance and development
